newsitem.title: LIBERIA: War-shattered Liberia set for watershed poll.
newsitem.headline: War-shattered Liberia set for watershed poll.

text.p: Liberia's war-weary people vote on Saturday in the first elections for 12 years, hoping to conclude a delicate transition from civil war to democracy.
The elections are taking place just before the 150th birthday on July 26 of the country, founded by freed American slaves in 1847 as Africa's first modern republic.

Seven years of a brutal civil war have scarred and traumatised the West African nation. The bloodshed and misery have haunted the international community which threw its weight behind a peace process brokered by West African states.

Some 500 international observers -- including 330 from the United Nations, 52 from the European Union, 41 from Atlanta- based Carter Center and 35 from the Organisation of African Unity -- are in Liberia monitoring the poll.
"We are here because we want to support Liberians who are tired of war and tired of violence," former U.S. president Jimmy Carter, leading the Carter Center team, told reporters.

"Tomorrow is a special day for Liberia and we urge each person who listens to this press conference to vote," Carter said at a joint news conference with the European Union and the pan-African organisation.

Twelve candidates including three converted warlords are running for president. One of the three, Charles Taylor, started the civil war but is seen as the frontrunner thanks to his charisma and superior resources.
The only woman candidate, former U.N. official Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf, is rated as Taylor's closest rival with potential to force the former warlord to a second round ballot.
Voters will also elect 26 senators and 64 lower house deputies in the poll based on proportional representation.
One month of campaigning climaxed in packed rallies in the war-battered capital Monrovia in the last two days to polling.
But the enthusiasm for democracy is being tempered by concern that the country could slide back into violence if losers refuse to accept the verdict of the electorate.
International effort is now concentrated on convincing losing candidates to agree to work with the winners.
"It's an extremely important step that is being taken by the people of Liberia to consolidate peace," said EU delegation chief, Dutch ambasador Antonius Speekenbrink.
He said Europe expected Liberians to elect "a government that can reconciliate and work for progress".
Carter pointedly included in his delegation former Benin president Nicephore Soglo. Like Carter he shares the distinction of winning one election and losing another.
Soglo who led regional negotiations on Liberia in 1994 as chairman of the ECOWAS West African grouping warned Liberians their problems would not end by the mere holding of elections.
"The difficult task is when you rebuild a country," he said.

The commander of the Nigerian-led ECOMOG West African peacekeeping force, General Victor Malu, said his troops had fanned out to take positions at each of the 1,900 polling stations to keep order and help with logistics.

"I am not expecting any trouble. I don't think anyone who has seen my troops all over the country will try anything," said Malu, who was singled out by Carter and EU officials for praise for disarming Liberia's 60,000 guerrillas.
Malu said a night curfew in force in Liberia since 1990 would be relaxed to allow voters to start queueing from 3.00 A.M. (0300 GMT) for the opening of polls at 7.00 A.M.
